text: I'd say it's a bit of both. It lets us stay in touch with friends and relatives abroad, which was impossible a generation ago. Yet a lot of online interaction is superficial, and some people end up feeling lonelier because they compare themselves with carefully edited images of others. Ultimately, it depends on whether it supplements real contact or replaces it.

questions.question: Has social media made people more connected or more isolated?

text: On balance, I believe so, provided it's used responsibly. AI can take over repetitive tasks and help doctors spot diseases earlier, which frees people up for more creative work. The risk is that we become overly dependent on it, or that it's used to spread misinformation. That's why clear rules and digital literacy are so important.

questions.question: Do you think artificial intelligence will make life better?

text: To some extent, yes. Young brains are still developing, and too much screen time can affect concentration and sleep. But I wouldn't ban technology altogether, since children need digital skills for the future. A sensible approach is agreeing on clear rules at home, such as no phones at the table, and setting a good example as parents.

text: I suspect face-to-face conversations will become rarer, replaced by virtual meetings and instant translation tools. Language barriers could largely disappear, which is exciting. However, I worry that we might lose subtler aspects of communication, like body language and tone. So while the convenience is undeniable, we'll need to make an effort to keep real human contact.
